summary: This section requires every share in a company with a share capital to have its own unique number so it can be easily identified. However, this rule does not apply to shares when a person holds the beneficial interest and their name is recorded in a depository. In short, physical shares need numbers, but dematerialized shares tracked by a depository do not.
points: Every share in a company that has share capital must have a distinctive number to identify it.
This rule applies to traditional or physical shares.
Shares held through a depository where a person is listed as the holder of a beneficial interest are exempt from this numbering rule.
example: Meera Textiles Private Limited issues physical shares to its early investors. According to the law, each of these physical share certificates must display a unique distinctive number so the company can track who owns every specific share. Later, investor Rohan decides to hold his shares electronically through a depository, where his name is entered as the holder of the beneficial interest in those shares. Because his shares are held in this depository system, the requirement for a physical distinctive number on those specific shares does not apply to them, making share tracking much easier in the digital format.

terms.meaning: The money a company raises by issuing shares to investors.
The right to enjoy the benefits of ownership of property or shares, even if another person or entity is the official registered owner.
An organization that holds securities in electronic form so they can be easily traded.

watch: A common confusion is assuming that all shares, including electronic ones in a depository, need distinctive numbers.
